title: Size matters: Sample size assessments for chronic wasting disease surveillance using an agent-based modeling framework
author: Belsare, Gompper, et al.

steps.title: Prepare forest cover ASCII grid
steps.instruction: Convert the forest‑cover data for the target region to a one‑square‑mile forest‑percentage grid and save it as an ASCII grid file (.asc). Record the ncols and nrows values shown in the file.

steps.title: Edit NODATA value
steps.instruction: Open the .asc file in a text editor and change the NODATA_value from 0 to –9999, then save the edited file back into the model’s data folder.

steps.title: Load new landscape into MOOvPOP
steps.instruction: In the MOOvPOP GUI, click the ‘Code’ tab, then the ‘Procedures’ tab and select ‘setup‑landscape’. Edit the code snippet to use the new landscape, setting resize‑world values to (ncols – 1) and (nrows – 1). On the ‘region’ tab right‑click, choose ‘Edit’, type the new region name, and finally click the ‘File’ tab → ‘Save’ to store the changes.

steps.title: Set sensitivity‑analysis parameters
steps.instruction: In MOOvPOPsurveillance, set the ‘adult‑prevalence’ slider to 0.01 (1 % prevalence in adult deer) and set both ‘%adult‑male‑harvest‑tested’ and ‘%adult‑female‑harvest‑tested’ sliders to 0.5 (50 % of adult harvest tested).

steps.title: Run baseline scenario
steps.instruction: Run the model with the default settings (no code changes) for 10 replicates, each consisting of 100 MOOvPOPsurveillance iterations, and record the output (e.g., CWDsurveillanceMO_bl1000.csv).

steps.title: Run alternate scenario
steps.instruction: Open the MOOvPOPsurveillance code, comment out lines 174‑181 and lines 815‑822 by adding a semicolon (;) at the start of each line, then run 10 replicates of 100 iterations and save the output (e.g., CWDsurveillanceMO_alt1000.csv).

Scenario 4 cluster96%: set lines 816 & 819 to 0.96 and lines 818 & 821 to 0.04.
Scenario 5 cluster94%: set lines 816 & 819 to 0.94 and lines 818 & 821 to 0.06.
Scenario 6 cluster92%: set lines 816 & 819 to 0.92 and lines 818 & 821 to 0.08.
Scenario 7 cluster90%: set lines 816 & 819 to 0.90 and lines 818 & 821 to 0.10.

steps.title: Collect and store output files
steps.instruction: For each of the 12 scenarios, keep the generated CSV files (e.g., CWDsurveillanceMO_bl1000.csv, CWDsurveillanceMO_alt1000.csv, nrs18‑nrs30 files, cl90‑cl98 files) in a designated results folder.

steps.title: Analyze results with R
steps.instruction: Download the R scripts from https://github.com/anyadoc/FranklinCWDsurveillance_Rcode (MOOvPOPsurvEvalSA_Rcode.R). Run the script to compute detection probabilities for the 12 prevalence‑sample‑size scenarios, compare them to hypergeometric approximations using a one‑sample t‑test, and reproduce Figure 6.

description: Surveillance for important wildlife diseases often relies on samples obtained from hunter-harvested animals. But sampling biases associated with harvest and spatiotemporal heterogeneities in disease distribution may result in biased estimates and erroneous inferences about disease presence and distribution. Yet, harvest-based sampling is widely used by wildlife agencies as it is a convenient and cost-effective mechanism of obtaining wildlife samples. Chronic wasting disease (CWD) surveillance of wild cervid populations in North America is a case in point. CWD is an emerging prion disease of cervids (including white-tailed deer Odocoileus virginianus, mule deer Odocoileus hemionus, and elk Cervus elaphus), and its continuing spread poses a serious long-term threat to the health of free-ranging cervid populations. In many states and provinces across North America, wildlife agencies obtain samples from harvested deer for CWD surveillance programs. We have developed an agent-based modeling framework that can be used as a decision-support tool for designing efficient harvest-based CWD surveillance strategies. The constituent models of this framework incorporate real-world heterogeneities in disease distribution, hunter harvest and harvest-based sampling, and can be used to determine population-specific sample sizes for reliable and prompt detection of the disease. The modeling framework was developed for, and in collaboration with, wildlife agency biologists and managers. Two agent-based models, MOOvPOP (MissOuri Odocoileus virginianus POPulation simulation model) and MOOvPOPsurveillance, constitute the framework. Both models are coded in NetLogo, an open source Java-based modeling environment, and model programs are freely available in the digital repository CoMSES Net Computational Model Library [2, 3].
